**Question 1 - Essay writing**

Write an essay in French of about 350 words on any ONE of the following topics.

**1.2** **Texte**

> - Lorsque le malade arrive, je prends les paramètres : la température, la tension, le pouls et le sang pour l'analyse (pour le cas de paludisme), en attendant que le médecin arrive.
> - C'est tout ce que vous, les infirmières, vous pouvez faire pour un cas d'urgence du palu ?
> - Si le docteur n'est pas disponible, je prescris des médicaments pour qu'on achète...
> Pendant ce temps l'état du malade s'empire.

**Question :**

Que faire pour rendre plus efficaces les services médicaux dans les centres hospitaliers de santé publique au Cameroun ? *(100 marks)*

**Plan de l'essai**

- Introduction : la scène du texte (urgence de paludisme, médecin absent, médicaments à acheter) ; problématique : comment rendre les services plus efficaces ?
- I. Renforcer et motiver le personnel (recrutement, gardes, formation, rémunération).
- II. Équiper les centres et approvisionner les pharmacies (médicaments, laboratoire, ambulances).
- III. Mieux gérer : lutte contre la corruption, assurance maladie, accueil des urgences, prévention.
- Conclusion : trois conditions réunies pour sauver le malade à temps.

**Essai modèle**

Ce court dialogue décrit une scène bien connue dans nos hôpitaux : un malade atteint de paludisme arrive en urgence, l'infirmière prend les paramètres, le médecin tarde, les médicaments manquent et l'état du patient s'aggrave. Comment rendre plus efficaces les services médicaux dans les centres hospitaliers de santé publique au Cameroun ? Je propose d'agir sur le personnel, sur les équipements et sur la gestion.

Il faut d'abord renforcer le personnel. Trop souvent, un seul médecin doit suivre des dizaines de patients, et il est absent quand l'urgence se présente. L'État doit recruter davantage de médecins, d'infirmiers et de sages-femmes, les répartir équitablement entre les villes et les villages, et organiser des gardes strictes, jour et nuit. Il doit aussi assurer la formation continue des soignants et les motiver par une rémunération correcte, afin qu'ils ne soient pas tentés de partir à l'étranger ou de travailler uniquement dans le privé.

Ensuite, il faut équiper les centres et approvisionner les pharmacies. Un hôpital sans médicaments, sans laboratoire et sans matériel de base ne peut pas soigner. Les pouvoirs publics doivent fournir en permanence les produits essentiels, notamment contre le paludisme, et moderniser les appareils de diagnostic. Cet effort éviterait la scène où l'on demande à la famille d'acheter les médicaments pendant que le malade s'affaiblit. Dans les zones rurales, où l'on parcourt parfois des kilomètres pour atteindre un centre de santé, des ambulances et des centres de proximité sauveraient de nombreuses vies.

Enfin, il faut améliorer la gestion et l'accueil. La lutte contre la corruption et les détournements est indispensable : les budgets doivent servir aux soins, et des contrôles réguliers doivent le garantir. On pourrait aussi instaurer une assurance maladie accessible à tous, afin qu'aucun patient ne soit refusé faute d'argent, et organiser un accueil rapide des urgences. Des campagnes de prévention, comme l'usage des moustiquaires, réduiraient en outre l'afflux de malades.

En somme, la qualité des soins repose sur des soignants présents et motivés, des centres bien équipés et une gestion honnête. Si ces trois conditions sont réunies, le malade du texte aura enfin la chance d'être sauvé à temps.

**1.3** Vous venez d'être élu Président de la République de votre pays. Quelles sont les stratégies que vous allez mettre sur pied pour atteindre les objectifs que vous vous êtes fixés ? *(100 marks)*

**Plan de l'essai**

- Introduction : le début d'un mandat, des objectifs (nation unie, prospère, juste) et la nécessité de stratégies.
- I. Éducation et jeunesse (écoles, enseignants, filières techniques).
- II. Économie (agriculture, petites entreprises, emploi des jeunes).
- III. Santé, infrastructures et gouvernance (hôpitaux, eau, routes, lutte contre la corruption, unité nationale).
- Conclusion : juger un Président à ses résultats.

**Essai modèle**

Être élu à la tête de l'État n'est pas un aboutissement, c'est le début d'une immense responsabilité. Maintenant que je viens d'être élu Président de la République de mon pays, je dois transformer mes promesses en actes. Les objectifs que je me suis fixés sont simples : bâtir une nation unie, prospère et juste. Pour les atteindre, je mettrai en place des stratégies précises dans l'éducation, l'économie, la santé et la gouvernance.

Ma première stratégie concernera la jeunesse, car un pays se construit par ses enfants. Je ferai construire des écoles et des laboratoires bien équipés, je recruterai et formerai des enseignants, et j'ouvrirai davantage de filières professionnelles et techniques, afin que chaque jeune acquière un métier utile à son pays.

Ma deuxième stratégie sera économique. Je soutiendrai l'agriculture, qui fait vivre la majorité de la population, en facilitant l'accès aux engrais, au crédit et aux routes rurales pour que les récoltes parviennent aux marchés. J'encouragerai aussi les petites entreprises et les investisseurs honnêtes, ce qui créera des emplois et réduira le chômage des jeunes diplômés. Je simplifierai aussi les démarches administratives pour que créer une entreprise ne devienne plus un parcours du combattant.

Ma troisième stratégie touchera la santé et les infrastructures : des hôpitaux équipés, de l'eau potable, de l'électricité et des routes entretenues dans toutes les régions, sans aucune distinction. Un citoyen qui se soigne, boit une eau saine et circule librement produit davantage et contribue mieux au développement de sa communauté.

Enfin, rien ne durera sans une gouvernance exemplaire. Je lutterai contre la corruption en rendant publics les budgets, en sanctionnant les détournements quel que soit le rang du coupable et en confiant les responsabilités aux plus compétents. Je veillerai aussi à l'unité nationale en dialoguant avec toutes les composantes de la société, car la paix est la condition de tout développement.

Ainsi, par l'éducation, l'économie, la santé et l'honnêteté dans la gestion, je m'efforcerai de tenir mes engagements. Un Président ne se juge pas à ses discours, mais aux résultats que le peuple constate dans sa vie quotidienne.

**Question 1 - Essay writing**

Write an essay in French of about 350 words on any ONE of the following topics.

**1.4** **Texte**

> **Lucie :** Nous ne bénéficions pas de ce revenu pour la famille car tu préfères le dilapider sur les femmes, donc je préfère mourir entre tes mains que de te laisser sortir.
>
> **Octave :** Laisse-moi sortir sinon tu t'exposes à la violence.

**Question :**

Dans beaucoup de foyers, les femmes font face à la violence conjugale. Après avoir présenté les manifestations de ce phénomène, vous direz ce qu'il y a lieu de faire pour mener une vie familiale harmonieuse. *(100 marks)*

**Plan de l'essai**

- Introduction : la scène du texte et la problématique (manifestations, remèdes).
- I. Les manifestations : violence physique, verbale et psychologique, économique, sociale ; conséquences sur les enfants.
- II. Que faire : dialogue et conseil conjugal, éducation au respect, autonomie financière de la femme, loi et associations, médiation des chefs traditionnels et religieux.
- Conclusion : respect, dialogue, justice et indépendance économique.

**Essai modèle**

Dans le texte, Lucie reproche à son mari de dilapider le revenu familial sur d'autres femmes, et Octave, au lieu de répondre, la menace de violence. Cette scène résume le drame de nombreux foyers où les femmes subissent la violence conjugale. Quelles en sont les manifestations, et que faire pour retrouver une vie familiale harmonieuse ?

La violence conjugale prend d'abord la forme de coups et de blessures : gifles, bousculades, parfois mutilations. Elle est aussi verbale et psychologique : insultes, humiliations, menaces, jalousie excessive. Elle est économique lorsque le mari refuse de donner l'argent nécessaire aux dépenses du ménage, gaspille le revenu du foyer à l'extérieur ou interdit à sa femme de travailler. Elle est enfin sociale quand l'épouse est isolée de ses proches ou chassée du domicile. Les enfants, témoins de ces scènes, en gardent des traumatismes durables.

Que faire pour y remédier ? Le premier remède est le dialogue : les époux doivent apprendre à discuter calmement de l'argent, de la fidélité et de l'éducation des enfants, au besoin avec l'aide d'un conseiller conjugal, d'un pasteur, d'un imam ou d'un parent respecté. Le deuxième est l'éducation : à l'école comme dans les lieux de culte, il faut enseigner le respect mutuel et l'égalité entre l'homme et la femme, et refuser l'idée qu'un mari a le droit de frapper. Le troisième est l'autonomie financière : une femme qui exerce une activité génératrice de revenus dépend moins de son conjoint et ose mieux se défendre. Le quatrième est la loi : l'État doit punir les auteurs de violences, protéger les victimes et soutenir les associations qui les accueillent. Les chefs traditionnels et religieux, très écoutés dans nos villages, peuvent aussi jouer un rôle de médiateurs.

La femme victime, enfin, ne doit pas se taire : elle doit en parler à des personnes de confiance et chercher de l'aide.

En conclusion, la violence conjugale détruit le couple et marque les enfants. Seuls le respect, le dialogue, la justice et l'indépendance économique de chacun permettront de bâtir des foyers où règnent la paix et l'harmonie.

**Question 2 - Translation**

Translate ALL the four texts.

**2.1 Translate into French**

> Jamah lived by his pen. But he was rather into reporting. He knew how to track down groups of bizarre humans, whose strange life he would describe in an alert style. For instance, he discovered in the forest, a mysterious family of old hermits on retirement, resolute bachelors. They were about thirty in number, living like ghosts in an old stony cave.

**Traduction modèle**

Jamah vivait de sa plume, mais il avait plutôt un penchant pour le reportage. Il savait dénicher des groupes d'êtres humains bizarres, dont il décrivait la vie étrange dans un style alerte. Par exemple, il avait découvert dans la forêt une famille mystérieuse de vieux ermites à la retraite, des célibataires endurcis. Ils étaient une trentaine, vivant comme des fantômes dans une vieille grotte rocailleuse.

**Difficultés de traduction**

| Difficulté | Piège | Bonne forme |
|---|---|---|
| « lived by his pen » | Calque : *vivait par sa plume* | *vivait de sa plume* (vivre de + nom) |
| « was rather into reporting » | Anglicisme : *était plutôt dans le reportage* | *avait plutôt un penchant pour le reportage* ou *s'intéressait plutôt au reportage* |
| « track down groups of bizarre humans » | *suivre à la trace* pris au sens policier, ou *humains* laissé tel quel | *dénicher* (ou *retrouver la trace de*) ; *êtres humains* ou *personnes bizarres* |
| « whose strange life he would describe » | Oublier le relatif ou le mettre mal : *desquels la vie* | pronom relatif *dont* : *dont il décrivait la vie étrange* ; *would* d'habitude ou de futur dans le passé : imparfait (ou conditionnel *décrirait*) |
| « in an alert style » | *style alert* (sans accord) ou *en alerte* | *dans un style alerte* (adjectif accordé, au sens de vif) |
| « he discovered... » | Mélanger présent et passé | Rester dans le passé : plus-que-parfait *il avait découvert* ou passé simple *il découvrit* |
| « resolute bachelors » | *célibataires résolus* | *célibataires endurcis* |
| « on retirement » | *en retirement*, *sur la retraite* | *à la retraite* |
| « about thirty in number » | *environ trente en nombre* | *une trentaine* ou *au nombre d'une trentaine* |
| « old stony cave » | *grotte pierreuse*, ordre des adjectifs anglais | *une vieille grotte rocailleuse* (adjectif de caractère après le nom, *vieille* avant) |

**Remarque de correction**

Le texte est un récit au passé : l'imparfait donne le décor (« vivait », « décrivait », « étaient »), le plus-que-parfait ou le passé simple marque la découverte. Une ponctuation erronée du sujet (« he discovered in the forest, a mysterious family ») est corrigée en français : on ne sépare pas le verbe de son complément par une virgule.

**Critères d'évaluation**

La traduction est notée sur les temps, les accords, le vocabulaire, la ponctuation et la syntaxe (100 points pour l'ensemble des quatre textes) : sens exact sans omission, correction grammaticale, naturel de la langue d'arrivée plutôt que mot à mot.

**Erreurs fréquentes**

1. Traduire mot à mot (*vivait par sa plume*, *célibataires résolus*, *grotte pierreuse*) au lieu de chercher l'expression française naturelle.
2. Mélanger les temps du récit (présent, passé composé, imparfait) ou oublier un élément (« in an alert style », « living like ghosts »).

**2.2 Translate into French**

> Sports occupies a greater part of leisure time. Apart from working hours some people spend time doing sports. It's however a pity for the sick who unfortunately cannot ride, jog, swim, do gymnastics or play. Although from time to time, the physically challenged practise less difficult sports, it is regrettable that they cannot do some of the most interesting exercises.

**Traduction modèle**

Le sport occupe une part plus importante du temps de loisir. En dehors des heures de travail, certaines personnes consacrent du temps à la pratique du sport. C'est cependant dommage pour les malades qui, malheureusement, ne peuvent ni faire du vélo, ni faire du jogging, ni nager, ni faire de la gymnastique, ni jouer. Bien que, de temps en temps, les personnes handicapées physiques pratiquent des sports moins difficiles, il est regrettable qu'elles ne puissent pas faire certains des exercices les plus intéressants.

**Difficultés de traduction**

| Difficulté | Piège | Bonne forme |
|---|---|---|
| « Sports occupies a greater part » | Accord ou nombre mal rendu ; *une plus grande partie* avec article mal choisi | *Le sport occupe une part plus importante* (ou *Les sports occupent*) ; *plus grande partie* accepté |
| « Apart from working hours » | *Apart de*, *à part des heures* | *En dehors des heures de travail* ou *Outre les heures de travail* |
| « spend time doing sports » | *dépenser du temps à faire des sports* | *passer du temps à faire du sport* ou *consacrer du temps au sport* (le verbe *dépenser* est un faux ami) |
| « It's however a pity for the sick » | *C'est pourtant une pitié pour* | *C'est cependant dommage pour les malades* (*pitié* n'est pas *pity* ici) |
| « unfortunately cannot » | Mauvaise place de l'adverbe ou *ne peuvent pas* répété | *qui, malheureusement, ne peuvent ni... ni...* (négation en *ne... ni... ni...*) |
| « ride, jog, swim, do gymnastics or play » | Oublier un verbe ; *faire de la gymnastique* écrit *faire gymnastique* | *faire du vélo* (ou *monter à cheval*, *ride* est ambigu), *faire du jogging* ou *courir*, *nager*, *faire de la gymnastique*, *jouer* |
| « the physically challenged » | *les physiquement défiés* (faux ami *challenged*) | *les personnes handicapées physiques* ou *les personnes à mobilité réduite* |
| « practise less difficult sports » | *pratiquer* orthographié à l'anglaise, ou *moins difficiles sports* | *pratiquent des sports moins difficiles* (accord du verbe avec *personnes*) |
| « it is regrettable that they cannot » | Indicatif après *il est regrettable que* : *ne peuvent pas* | subjonctif : *il est regrettable qu'elles ne puissent pas* |
| « some of the most interesting exercises » | *quelques-uns des plus intéressants exercices* | *certains des exercices les plus intéressants* (superlatif relatif : article + *plus* + adjectif après le nom) |

**Remarque de correction**

Le sujet imprime « Sports occupies » (verbe au singulier) : *Le sport occupe* et *Les sports occupent* sont tous deux acceptés. Les verbes *ride* et *play* n'ont pas de complément : on choisit une formule naturelle en français (*faire du vélo* ou *monter à cheval* ; *jouer*).

**Critères d'évaluation**

La traduction est notée sur les temps, les accords, le vocabulaire, la ponctuation et la syntaxe (100 points pour l'ensemble des quatre textes) : sens exact sans omission, correction grammaticale, naturel de la langue d'arrivée plutôt que mot à mot.

**Erreurs fréquentes**

1. Utiliser l'indicatif après *il est regrettable que* (le subjonctif *puissent* est obligatoire) et oublier la double négation *ne... ni... ni*.
2. Tomber dans les faux amis : *dépenser du temps* (passer ou consacrer), *challenged* (défié), *pitié* pour *pity* (dommage).

| Difficulté | Piège | Bonne forme |
|---|---|---|
| « hériter d'une femme » | *inherit of a woman* (préposition française recopiée) | *inherit a wife* (verbe transitif direct) ; *femme* = *wife* dans ce contexte |
| « s'approprier » | *appropriate* seul, ou *to approprier* | *to take possession of*, *to take over* ou *to appropriate* |
| « sa belle femme » | *his beautiful woman* | *his beautiful wife* (*femme* = épouse, pas *woman*) |
| « ses biens et ses dettes » | *his goods and his debts* (*goods* = marchandises) | *his property* (ou *his possessions*, *his assets*) *and his debts* |
| « en vue de les protéger et d'en tirer profit » | *with a view to protect* (infinitif après *to*) | *with a view to protecting them and profiting from them* (gérondif après *with a view to*) ; *en* = *from them* |
| « comme le défunt l'aurait souhaité » | *like the deceased would wish* | *as the deceased would have wished* (conditionnel passé = *would have* + participe) |
| « sans qu'on s'en rende compte » | *without that we realise* | *without anyone realising it* ou *without people noticing* |
| « revêtant une signification » | *wearing a meaning* | *taking on* ou *assuming a meaning* (participe présent) |
| « notoire » | *notorious* (sens péjoratif) | *well known* ; *notorious* est un faux ami partiel, il suppose une mauvaise réputation |
| « de nos jours » | *of our days* | *nowadays* ou *today* |

**Remarque de correction**

Le texte décrit une pratique sociale (héritage de l'épouse) : le registre reste neutre et informatif. Pour *notoire*, on privilégie *well known* ; *notorious* est toléré si le contexte critique la pratique, ce que « totalement différente » laisse entendre.

**Critères d'évaluation**

La traduction est notée sur les temps, les accords, le vocabulaire, la ponctuation et la syntaxe (100 points pour l'ensemble des quatre textes) : sens exact sans omission, correction grammaticale, naturel de la langue d'arrivée plutôt que mot à mot.

**Erreurs fréquentes**

1. Calquer les prépositions et les structures françaises (*inherit of*, *with a view to protect*, *without that*) au lieu d'employer les constructions anglaises.
2. Se tromper sur les faux amis : *femme* rendu par *woman* au lieu de *wife*, *biens* par *goods*, *notoire* par *notorious* sans nuance.

**Question 2 - Translation**

Translate ALL the four texts.

**2.4 Traduire en anglais**

> C'était la récréation. Les élèves jouaient dans la cour lorsqu'il y a eu un bruit assourdissant. Une bombe artisanale s'était détonnée non loin d'une agence de transport routier. Tout le monde a pris fuite dans toutes les directions. Dès lors, les enseignants ne pouvaient plus continuer avec les cours comme les apprenants ne pouvaient plus prendre leur courage pour rentrer en classe.

**Traduction modèle**

It was break time. The pupils were playing in the schoolyard when there was a deafening noise. A homemade bomb had gone off not far from a road transport agency. Everybody ran away in all directions. From then on, the teachers could no longer continue with their lessons, since the learners could no longer find the courage to go back to class.

**Difficultés de traduction**

| Difficulté | Piège | Bonne forme |
|---|---|---|
| « C'était la récréation » | *It was the recreation* | *It was break time* ou *playtime* (*recess* en anglais américain) |
| « jouaient dans la cour » | *played* (simple past) | *were playing in the schoolyard* (action en cours : past continuous) ; *cour* = *schoolyard*, *playground* |
| « lorsqu'il y a eu un bruit assourdissant » | *when it had a deafening noise* | *when there was a deafening noise* ou *when a deafening noise was heard* |
| « bombe artisanale » | *artisanal bomb* | *homemade bomb* ou *improvised explosive device* |
| « s'était détonnée » | *was detonated* ou *had detonate* | *had gone off* ou *had exploded* (plus-que-parfait : l'explosion précède le bruit relaté) |
| « agence de transport routier » | *agency of road transport* | *road transport agency* (ordre anglais : nom déterminant avant le nom) |
| « Tout le monde a pris fuite » | *All the world fled* | *Everybody ran away* ou *Everyone fled* (verbe au singulier, *tout le monde* = *everybody*) |
| « Dès lors » | *Since then* sans nuance | *From then on* ou *As a result* selon le sens de conséquence |
| « ne pouvaient plus continuer avec les cours » | *could not more continue* | *could no longer continue with their lessons* (*no longer* avant le verbe lexical) |
| « apprenants » | *apprentices* (faux ami) | *learners*, *pupils* ou *students* |
| « prendre leur courage pour rentrer en classe » | *take their courage to enter in class* | *find* ou *summon up the courage to go back to class* (*go back to class*, jamais *enter in class*) |

**Remarque de correction**

Le texte imprimé contient « a pris fuite » (pour *a pris la fuite*) et « s'était détonnée » : ces tournures sont traduites par leur sens (*ran away*, *had gone off*). Le « comme » de la dernière phrase est causal : *since* ou *as*.

**Critères d'évaluation**

La traduction est notée sur les temps, les accords, le vocabulaire, la ponctuation et la syntaxe (100 points pour l'ensemble des quatre textes) : sens exact sans omission, correction grammaticale, naturel de la langue d'arrivée plutôt que mot à mot.

**Erreurs fréquentes**

1. Choisir un mauvais temps : *played* au lieu de *were playing* pour une action en cours interrompue, ou *exploded* au passé simple au lieu du plus-que-parfait.
2. Faux amis et calques : *apprenants* rendu par *apprentices*, *bombe artisanale* par *artisanal bomb*, *prendre leur courage* par *take their courage*.

**1.** A career in society that is related to Geology is;

a) Petrol vendor.
b) Environmental consultant.
c) An electrical engineer.
d) A plumber.

Environmental consultants assess ground conditions, pollution, water and land use, which needs geological knowledge. A petrol vendor, an electrical engineer and a plumber do not need to apply geology to their trade.

**Answer: B.**

**2.** A discontinuity that separates the outer core from the inner core is called;

a) Conrad.
b) Lehman.
c) Moho.
d) Gutenberg.

The Lehmann discontinuity (printed "Lehman") lies at about 5150 km depth between the liquid outer core and the solid inner core. Conrad separates upper and lower crust, the Moho separates crust and mantle, and the Gutenberg discontinuity separates mantle and outer core.

**Answer: B.**

**3.** What is the physical state of the Earth's outer core?

a) Liquid.
b) Solid.
c) Plastic.
d) Liquid and solid.

S-waves do not pass through the outer core, which shows that it is liquid (molten iron and nickel). The inner core is solid because of the very high pressure; the mantle is the layer that is partly plastic.

**Answer: A.**

**4.** Lowlands found on the moon's surface are called;

a) Terrae.
b) Rille.
c) Crater.
d) Maria.

The dark, smooth lowland plains of the Moon, filled with basaltic lava, are the maria (singular mare). The bright highlands are the terrae, a rille is a long channel-like valley and a crater is a bowl-shaped depression.

**Answer: D.**

**5.** Which of the following earthquake waves are Transverse waves?

a) Primary.
b) Secondary.
c) Primary and secondary.
d) Rayleigh.

Secondary (S) waves make the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel, so they are transverse waves. Primary (P) waves are longitudinal (compressional). Rayleigh waves are surface waves with a rolling, elliptical motion.

**Answer: B.**

**6.** An example of a light coloured, coarse-grained, acid igneous rock is;

a) Granite.
b) Rhyolite.
c) Pumice.
d) Syenite.

Granite is coarse-grained (intrusive) and rich in quartz and feldspar, so it is light coloured and acid. Rhyolite is acid but fine-grained, pumice is a frothy volcanic glass, and syenite is an intermediate rock with little or no quartz.

**Answer: A.**

**7.** Which layer of the Earth is rich in peridotites?

a) Inner core.
b) Upper crust.
c) Lower crust.
d) Mantle.

Peridotite (rich in olivine and pyroxene) is the main rock of the upper mantle. The cores are iron-nickel, the upper crust is mainly granitic and the lower crust mainly basaltic.

**Answer: D.**

**8.** The rapid downslope movement of soil and rock as a result of gravity is;

a) Rock Fall.
b) Creep.
c) Landslide.
d) Earth Flow.

A landslide is the rapid downslope movement of a mass of soil and rock under gravity. Creep is very slow, a rock fall involves only rock falling freely from a cliff, and an earth flow is a more fluid movement of soil.

**Answer: C.**

**9.** What type of plate boundary exist in the mid - oceanic ridge?

a) Convergent.
b) Divergent.
c) Destructive.
d) Conservative.

At a mid-oceanic ridge two plates move apart and new oceanic crust is created: this is a divergent (constructive) boundary. Convergent and destructive boundaries are where plates collide, and conservative boundaries are where they slide past each other.

**Answer: B.**

**10.** The name of a metamorphic rock use in roofing is;

a) Slate.
b) Gneiss.
c) Quartzite.
d) Phyllite.

Slate splits easily into thin, flat, durable sheets (slaty cleavage), so it is the rock used for roofing tiles. Gneiss and quartzite are too coarse or too massive, and phyllite is a shinier, less regular rock.

**Answer: A.**

**11.** Volcanoes that show evidence of recent eruptions are said to be:

a) Extinct.
b) Dormant.
c) Passive.
d) Active.

A volcano that has erupted recently, or is erupting now, is active. A dormant volcano is quiet but may erupt again, and an extinct volcano is not expected to erupt again.

**Answer: D.**

**12.** The most important factor responsible for contact metamorphism;

a) Pressure.
b) Chemical fluids.
c) Heat.
d) Hydrostatic stress.

Contact (thermal) metamorphism occurs around an intrusion of magma where the country rock is baked by heat, with little pressure. Pressure is the main factor in regional metamorphism.

**Answer: C.**

**13.** Study the diagram of the fault (Figure 1) and answer question 13.

![Figure 1: block diagram of a near-vertical fault with horizontal movement arrows on the top surface. Used for question 13.](/media/figures/cm/gce-ol-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.webp)

*Figure 1: a block diagram cut by a near-vertical fault; two arrows on the top surface show the two sides moving horizontally in opposite directions, and the dark marker beds are displaced sideways.*

Identify the type of fault above.

a) Normal.
b) Reverse.
c) Tear.
d) Oblique.

The arrows lie in the horizontal plane and the marker bands are shifted sideways, so the movement is horizontal along the strike of the fault, with almost no vertical displacement. This is a tear (strike-slip, wrench) fault. A normal or reverse fault shows vertical movement down or up the fault plane, and an oblique fault shows both.

**Answer: C.**

**14.** An instrument that is used in measuring earthquake is called;

a) Seismograph.
b) Seismogram.
c) Clinometer.
d) Ritcher scale.

A seismograph is the instrument that records ground motion. The seismogram is the record it produces, the clinometer measures dip, and the Richter scale is a scale of magnitude, not an instrument.

**Answer: A.**

**15.** Which of the following is a stream erosional process?

a) Hydraulic action.
b) Blasting.
c) Saltation.
d) Traction.

Hydraulic action (the force of water on the banks and bed) is an erosional process. Saltation and traction are ways in which a stream transports its load, and blasting is not a stream process.

**Answer: A.**

**16.** An example of a feature produced by wind deposition is;

a) Pot holes.
b) Zeugens.
c) Loess.
d) Ventifacts.

Loess is a fine windblown silt deposit. Zeugen and ventifacts are produced by wind erosion (abrasion), and pot holes are formed by river erosion.

**Answer: C.**

**17.** A property in rocks that allows the movement of water through interconnected pore spaces is known as;

a) Porosity.
b) Permeability.
c) Perviousity.
d) Semi -porosity.

Permeability is the ability of a rock to let water pass through connected pores. Porosity is only the proportion of pore space, which can be high (clay) without the pores being connected.

**Answer: B.**

**18.** Which of the following represents dwarf planets?

*Options as printed:* A) Deimos and Phobos.   B) Makemake and Haumea.   C) Pluto and Eris.   D) Mercury and Venus.

Deimos and Phobos are moons of Mars, and Mercury and Venus are planets. Both Pluto and Eris and also Makemake and Haumea are dwarf planets, so the intended single key (Pluto and Eris) cannot be established from the options.

**Intended answer: C (Pluto and Eris).**

**19.** Which of the following environmental factors promote the formation of an exfoliation dome?

a) Pressure release.
b) Variation in temperature.
c) Frost action.
d) Animal activities.

Exfoliation domes form when erosion removes overlying rock, the pressure on the deep rock (granite) is released, it expands and peels off in curved sheets. Temperature variation and frost action are other weathering agents but are not the cause of dome formation.

**Answer: A.**

**20.** Fractures in rocks that do not show any observable displacements are called?

a) Faults.
b) Joints.
c) Folds.
d) Cleavage.

A joint is a fracture along which there has been no visible movement. A fault shows displacement, a fold is a bend, and cleavage is a property of a mineral or the splitting of a metamorphic rock.

**Answer: B.**

**21.** Identify a mineral with a hardness of 7.

a) Apatite.
b) Calcite.
c) Quartz.
d) Orthoclase.

On Mohs' scale quartz is 7, apatite 5, calcite 3 and orthoclase 6.

**Answer: C.**

**22.** A strip of beach connecting the main land to an island is referred to as;

a) Tombolo.
b) Spit.
c) Barrier island.
d) Bay.

A tombolo is a ridge of sand or shingle joining an island to the mainland. A spit is attached to land at one end only, a barrier island is separated from the land by a lagoon, and a bay is a coastal indentation.

**Answer: A.**

**23.** Which igneous rock is the plutonic equivalence of basalt?

a) Peridotite.
b) Granite.
c) Granodiorite.
d) Gabbro.

Basalt (extrusive, basic) has the same composition as gabbro (intrusive, coarse-grained). Granite and granodiorite are acid to intermediate, and peridotite is ultrabasic.

**Answer: D.**

**24.** The ancient sea that separated Laurasia and Gondwanaland is;

a) Tethys.
b) Pathalasia.
c) Dead sea.
d) Red sea.

The Tethys Sea lay between the northern continent Laurasia and the southern continent Gondwanaland. Panthalassa was the ocean surrounding Pangaea; the Dead Sea and Red Sea are modern.

**Answer: A.**

**25.** Ancient organisms preserved in rocks are known as;

a) Fossils.
b) Coal.
c) Petroleum.
d) Corals.

Fossils are the remains or traces of ancient organisms preserved in rocks. Coal and petroleum are fuels derived from organic matter, and corals are only one group of organisms.

**Answer: A.**

**26.** What stage of a river profile is the cross section of the valley V-shaped?

a) Youthful.
b) Middle.
c) Mature.
d) Old.

In the youthful (upper) stage the river cuts downwards (vertical erosion) and forms a steep V-shaped valley. In later stages lateral erosion widens the valley and builds a flood plain.

**Answer: A.**

**27.** Which of the following dating methods is the most accurate?

a) Relative.
b) Absolute.
c) Superposition.
d) Cross cutting relationship.

Absolute (radiometric) dating gives a numerical age in years, with a stated margin of error. Superposition and cross-cutting relationships are principles of relative dating, which only gives the order of events.

**Answer: B.**

**28.** An example of a coarse grained sedimentary rock is;

a) Sandstone.
b) Conglomerate.
c) Granite.
d) Shale.

Conglomerate is made of pebbles and gravel (coarse clasts, over 2 mm). Sandstone is medium-grained, shale is fine-grained and granite is igneous.

**Answer: B.**

**29.** The silica content in acid magma is;

a) 52-65%.
b) 45-52%.
c) Less than 45%.
d) Greater than 65%.

Acid magma has more than 65% (about 66% or more) silica. Intermediate magma has 52-65%, basic 45-52% and ultrabasic less than 45%.

**Answer: D.**

**30.** The lowest permissible metallic deposit of an ore is called;

*Options as printed:* A) Gangue.   B) Concentration factor.   C) Tenor.   D) Clarke of an ore.

In the usual classroom definition, the tenor of an ore is its metal content, and the lowest permissible tenor is the minimum that can be mined at a profit. Gangue is the worthless mineral, and the clarke is the average crustal abundance of an element. The concentration factor (grade divided by clarke) could also be argued, so the key is not certain.

c) Inlier.

The oldest rock is in the centre and the younger beds dip away from it on all sides, which defines a dome. In a basin the youngest rock is at the centre and the beds dip inwards. An inlier is an older rock surrounded by younger rock and an outlier is a younger rock surrounded by older rock; both are outcrop patterns produced by erosion, not structures.

**32.** An igneous texture with grain size greater than 5mm is referred to as;

a) Phaneritic.
b) Microphaneritic.
c) Aphanitic.
d) Glassy.

Phaneritic texture means that the crystals are large enough to be seen with the naked eye (intrusive rocks, grains of 1 mm and more). Aphanitic grains are too small to see, microphaneritic grains are small and just visible, and glassy rocks have no crystals. Phaneritic is therefore the best of the four options.

**Answer: A.**

**33.** Unconformities are used to identify;

a) Depositional features.
b) Landslide scarp.
c) Transportation direction.
d) Erosional surfaces.

An unconformity is a surface of erosion or non-deposition between older and younger rocks, so it marks a gap in the geological record and an ancient erosional surface.

**Answer: D.**

**34.** The point of origin of an earthquake is called;

a) Epicenter.
b) Crust.
c) Mantle.
d) Focus.

The focus (hypocentre) is the point underground where the rupture starts. The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.

**Answer: D.**

**35.** Which concept explains the constant movement of oceanic floors away from the mid- oceanic ridges?

a) Continental drift.
b) Sea-floor spreading.
c) Waves.
d) Tides.

Sea-floor spreading is the process by which new crust formed at the ridge moves away on both sides. Continental drift describes the movement of the continents, not the creation of ocean floor; waves and tides do not move the floor.

**Answer: B.**

**36.** Which of the following differentiates a brachiopod from a bivalve respectively?

Option B is a correct difference: a brachiopod has a dorsal and a ventral valve (up and down) and a bivalve has a left and a right valve. Option D is also a defensible difference (brachiopod valves are unequal in size, bivalve valves are mirror images), so the question has two valid options and no single key can be given.

A mineral with well-developed crystal faces is euhedral. Anhedral crystals have no faces, subhedral crystals have partly developed faces, and octahedral is a specific crystal form.

**38.** Which groups of rocks do we commonly find Petroleum?

b) Sedimentary.
c) Metamorphic.
d) Foliated.

Petroleum forms from organic matter buried in marine sediments and migrates into porous sedimentary reservoir rocks (sandstone, limestone). Heat and pressure in igneous and metamorphic rocks destroy or prevent it.

The triclinic system has only a centre of symmetry (or none) and no plane or axis of symmetry, and its three axes are unequal and mutually oblique. The tetragonal, cubic and monoclinic systems all have planes and/or axes of symmetry.

**41.** The study of the nature and origin of rocks is known as;

b) Petrology.

Petrology is the branch of geology that studies rocks: their composition, texture and origin. Geology is the whole science and structural geology studies rock deformation.

**42.** Secondary minerals that bind particles together in sedimentary rocks are called;

a) Matrix.
b) Sediments.
c) Cement.
d) Clay stones.

Cement (silica, calcite, iron oxide) is the secondary mineral precipitated between grains that binds them together. The matrix is the fine material that fills the spaces between grains, not a binding mineral.

a) Coarse grained, well sorted.
b) Rounded grains, particle sizes greater than 2mm.
c) Fine grained, well sorted and rounded grains.
d) Coarse and angular grains.

Breccia is made of coarse, angular fragments, because they have not been transported far. Rounded grains over 2 mm describe conglomerate.

**48.** Specific locations on a map are gotten by the help of;

b) Grid reference.

**49.** A gas when abundant in the atmosphere can cause global warming is;

a) Helium.
b) Ozone.
c) Argon.
d) Carbondioxide.

Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas: it absorbs infrared radiation and traps heat. Helium and argon are inert and do not absorb heat, and ozone high in the atmosphere protects against UV radiation.

**50.** A structure having dip arrows dipping towards each other, with the youngest bed at the core represents;

b) Syncline.
c) Antiform.
d) Synform.

Beds that dip towards each other form a trough, and a trough with the youngest bed in the core is a syncline. An anticline has the oldest beds in the core and beds dipping away. A synform is a trough-shaped fold whose age order is unknown, so it is not the specific answer.

**a.** Define the following terms as used in seismology.

**(i) Earthquake magnitude** is a measure of the amount of energy released at the source (focus) of an earthquake. It is expressed on a logarithmic scale (the Richter scale or the moment magnitude scale), so each whole number represents about 32 times more energy than the one below.

**(ii) Earthquake epicentre** is the point on the Earth's surface vertically above the focus (the point underground where the rocks first break). It is where the shaking is usually strongest.

2. The two valves are usually **mirror images** of each other (equivalve), with the plane of symmetry passing between them.
3. Each valve has an **umbo** (the oldest part of the shell) and concentric growth lines.
4. The valves are held by a hinge with teeth and sockets, and closed by adductor muscles that leave scars inside the shell.
5. They are soft-bodied molluscs without a head, living in water (marine or freshwater).

4. **Solution**: dissolving of soluble minerals such as rock salt in water.
5. **Hydration**: absorption of water by minerals, e.g. anhydrite changing to gypsum.

**a.** Define the following terms as used in Crystallography:

(i) Crystal face: (2 marks)

(ii) Crystal form: (2 marks)

**(i) Crystal face** is a flat, smooth natural surface that bounds a crystal; it is the outside expression of the regular internal arrangement of the atoms.

**(ii) Crystal form** is a set of crystal faces that are all alike in size, shape and relation to the crystallographic axes, because they are related by the symmetry of the crystal (e.g. the six square faces of a cube make one form).

**b.** Differentiate between cleavage and fracture of a mineral.

(2 marks)

**Cleavage** is the tendency of a mineral to break along smooth, flat, parallel planes of weakness in its atomic structure (e.g. mica, calcite, halite).

**Fracture** is the way a mineral breaks in directions that are *not* planes of weakness, giving irregular or curved surfaces (e.g. the conchoidal, shell-like fracture of quartz).

So cleavage gives regular, flat, repeatable surfaces, while fracture gives irregular surfaces.

**c.** Distinguish between marine transgression and regression.

(2 marks)

**Marine transgression** is the advance (spread) of the sea over the land, caused by a rise in sea level or a sinking of the land; the shoreline moves inland and finer, deeper-water sediments are deposited over coarser, shallow-water ones.

**Marine regression** is the retreat of the sea from the land, caused by a fall in sea level or an uplift of the land; the shoreline moves seaward and coarser, shallow-water sediments are deposited over finer ones, leaving land exposed.

**d.** State TWO effects of earthquakes.

(2 marks)

1. Collapse of buildings, bridges and roads, causing loss of life and injuries.
2. Landslides and rock falls, and cracks (fissures) opening in the ground.
3. Tsunamis when the epicentre is under the sea.
4. Fires and floods from broken gas pipes, electric cables and dams.
5. Liquefaction of loose, wet soil.

**1.** The term Logic is derived from the Greek word "Logos" which means?

*Options as printed:* A) Organon.   B) Discourse.   C) Thinking.   D) Reasoning.

"Logos" is a Greek word with several accepted meanings: word, discourse, thought and reason. Three of the four printed options (Discourse, Thinking, Reasoning) are all given in standard textbooks as the meaning of "logos", so the question cannot be marked reliably. "Organon" is wrong: it is the title Aristotle's logical works received later, not the root of the word.

**Intended answer: "Logos" means word, discourse, thought or reason (Organon is the only wrong option).**

**2.** The most appropriate reason why the study of Logic is important is that it enables one to:

*Options as printed:* A) Gain clarity and precision in speech.   B) Perceive the coherence and incoherence of terms.   C) Investigate and detect true argument.   D) Weigh the pros and cons of propositions.

Logic is important because it gives standards for telling good reasoning from bad reasoning, which includes seeing whether an argument is valid and weighing the reasons for and against a claim. Option A (clarity of speech) is a by-product, B speaks of "terms" when coherence concerns propositions and arguments, C wrongly speaks of a "true" argument (arguments are valid or invalid, not true or false), and D is defensible. The printed key cannot be fixed with certainty, so the question is left open.

**Intended answer: Logic enables us to distinguish valid from invalid reasoning and to weigh reasons for and against a claim (D is the closest option).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**3.** "A form five boy was caught cheating in an exam, and it was later concluded that all form five boys are exam cheats". This is an example of:

a) Inductive Reasoning.
b) Logical reasoning.
c) Analogical Reasoning.
d) Deductive Reasoning.

The conclusion about ALL form five boys is drawn from one observed case. Reasoning from particular cases to a general statement is induction (here a hasty generalisation). It is not deductive, because the conclusion goes beyond what the premise guarantees, and it is not analogical, because no comparison between two things is made. "Logical reasoning" is too general to be a type.

**Answer: A.**

**4.** Which of the following Laws of Thought is expressed in the formula A=A?

a) Principle of Excluded Middle.
b) Principle of Contradiction.
c) Principle of Identity.
d) Principle of non-contradiction.

The formula $A = A$ says that a thing is the same as itself: this is the Principle (Law) of Identity. Excluded Middle is $A \vee \sim A$, and Contradiction (non-contradiction) is $\sim(A \cdot \sim A)$.

**Answer: C.**

**5.** The Operation of the Mind in which ideas are compared is known as:

a) Thinking.
b) Reasoning.
c) Abstraction.
d) Judging.

The three operations of the mind are simple apprehension (forming ideas), judgment (comparing two ideas and affirming or denying one of the other) and reasoning (passing from judgments to a new judgment). Comparing ideas is judging. Reasoning compares judgments, and abstraction forms ideas.

**Answer: D.**

**6.** Identify the fields that both deal with thinking:

a) Logic and Psychology.
b) Logic and History.
c) Logic and Law.
d) Logic and Science.

Psychology studies how people actually think (the mental process), while Logic studies how people ought to think correctly (the standards of valid reasoning). Both therefore deal with thinking. History, Law and Science use reasoning but do not take thinking itself as their subject.

**Answer: A.**

**7.** The terms "Teacher and Learner" are adequately known as:

a) Contrary.
b) Correlative.
c) Contradictory.
d) Positive.

Correlative terms are terms that imply each other: there is no teacher without a learner and no learner without a teacher (like husband and wife, parent and child). Contrary terms are extremes of one scale (hot and cold) and contradictory terms exclude each other with nothing in between (guilty and not guilty).

**Answer: B.**

**8.** Two Terms in which one negates the other are considered as:

a) Correlative Terms.
b) Negative Terms.
c) Contradictory Terms.
d) Contrary Terms.

Contradictory terms are a term and its negation (healthy and non-healthy): they cannot both apply to the same thing and they cannot both be denied of it. Contrary terms (black and white) cannot both apply but both can be denied (grey), so one does not simply negate the other.

**Answer: C.**

**9.** The statement of an essential attribute of terms is known as:

a) Denotation.
b) Concept.
c) Extension.
d) Connotation.

The connotation (intension) of a term is the set of essential attributes that a thing must have to be called by that term. Denotation (extension) is the set of things to which the term applies.

**Answer: D.**

**10.** The Function of language to cause or prevent action is:

a) Informative.
b) Directory.
c) Expressive.
d) Cognitive.

The function of language that aims to cause or prevent action (commands, requests, instructions) is the directive function. The printed word "Directory" is a misprint of "Directive" and is the only option that matches. Informative and cognitive language conveys information, and expressive language shows feelings.

**Answer: B.**

**11.** Which Language Function is expressed in the sentence, "Oh what a wonderful party!"?

a) Emotive.
b) Directory.
c) Informative.
d) Cognitive.

The sentence expresses the speaker's feelings. This is the emotive (expressive) function of language. It gives no information to be tested and issues no command.

**Answer: A.**

**12.** Identify from below that which is False of the relation between Language and Thought:

a) Language permits one to express ideas.
b) Language expresses thoughts.
c) Language dominates over thoughts.
d) Language can contextualize ideas.

Language is the vehicle of thought: it permits us to express ideas, expresses thoughts and can place ideas in a context. It does not dominate thought, because thought comes first and language serves it. Option C is therefore the false statement.

**Answer: C.**

**13.** A word or words used in explaining a term is/are known as:

a) Logical Division.
b) Definiendum.
c) Definition.
d) Definiens.

In a definition, the term to be defined is the definiendum and the word or words that explain it are the definiens. Only D matches "words used in explaining a term".

**Answer: D.**

**14.** A kind of Definition which gives meaning to a brand new term is:

a) Synonymous Definition.
b) Stipulative Definition.
c) Lexical Definition.
d) Theoretical Definition.

A stipulative definition assigns a meaning to a new term (or a new meaning to an old one), as when a scientist names a new discovery. A lexical definition reports the existing dictionary use of a word.

**Answer: B.**

**15.** The expression, "Logic is everywhere, even in the air we breathe" most adequately represents:

a) Persuasive Definition
b) Stipulative Definition
c) Nominal Definition
d) Descriptive Definition

The sentence uses emotionally loaded, rhetorical language to make us feel that logic matters, rather than to state the exact meaning of the word. A definition meant to influence attitudes in this way is a persuasive definition.

**Answer: A.**

**16.** Which Fallacy is committed when a Definition is stated in Figurative language?

a) Obscure Definition.
b) Incongruous Definition.
c) Extraneous Definition.
d) Circular Definition.

A good definition must be clear. A definition in figurative, vague or ambiguous language ("Man is the glory of creation") hides the meaning instead of showing it: this is the fault of obscurity, the obscure definition. A circular definition uses the term in its own definiens.

**Answer: A.**

**17.** In Logical Division the Species into which the Genus is subdivided is adequately called:

a) Totum Divisum.
b) Fundamentum Divisionis.
c) Membra Dividentia.
d) Definiens.

A logical division has three parts: the totum divisum (the whole or genus divided), the fundamentum divisionis (the basis of the division) and the membra dividentia (the dividing members, i.e. the species). The species are the membra dividentia.

**Answer: C.**

**18.** An assertion which is capable of being True or False is known as a:

*Options as printed:* A) Statement.   B) Proposition.   C) Sentence.   D) Phrase.

An assertion that is either true or false is called a proposition in traditional logic and a statement in modern logic; the two words are used for the same thing in many textbooks. A sentence can be a question or a command and a phrase asserts nothing. Because both A and B are defensible, the question cannot be marked reliably.

**Intended answer: a proposition (also called a statement).**

**19.** A Proposition which is a straight forward affirmative or negative statement without a condition is best described as:

a) Hypothetical proposition.
b) Disjunctive.
c) Modal.
d) Categorical.

A categorical proposition asserts or denies something unconditionally ("All men are mortal"). A hypothetical proposition has an "if ... then" condition, a disjunctive one an "either ... or", and a modal one states a mode (possible, necessary).

**Answer: D.**

**20.** A Proposition which asserts that "the members of one class are totally or partially excluded from another class", is most appropriately known as:

a) Negative Proposition.
b) Particular Proposition.
c) Affirmative Proposition.
d) Universal Proposition.

Exclusion of one class from another, totally (E: No S is P) or partially (O: Some S is not P), is what a negative proposition does. An affirmative proposition includes a class in another, and universal and particular describe quantity, not quality.

**Answer: A.**

**21.** The statement "Teachers are Intelligent Persons" can be translated into its optimum logical form as:

a) Some teachers are intelligent persons.
b) Some intelligent persons are teachers.
c) All teachers are intelligent persons.
d) All intelligent persons are teachers.

An unquantified subject with an affirmative predicate is normally read as universal: "Teachers are intelligent persons" becomes the A proposition "All teachers are intelligent persons" (All S are P). Option D reverses subject and predicate, and A and B weaken the claim to particular propositions.

**Answer: C.**

**22.** Identify the vowel corresponding to the Proposition whose Predicate Term is distributed and Subject Term is undistributed:

b) I
c) A
d) O

**23.** Which portion is shaded in representing the "A" Proposition on the Venn diagram?

a) $\bar{S}P$
b) $\overline{SP}$
c) $S\bar{P}$

The A proposition "All S are P" says that nothing is S and not P, so the part of S lying outside P is shaded as empty. That region is $S\bar{P}$. $SP$ is the overlap (shaded for the E proposition), and $\bar{S}P$ is the part of P outside S.

**24.** Which of the following is true of Immediate Inference?

a) The conclusion follows from two premises.
b) The process begins from two terms.
c) The process involves an intermediary.
d) The conclusion follows from the three terms.

Immediate inference draws a conclusion from a single proposition, with no middle term or second premise. A, C and D describe mediate inference (the syllogism), so they are false. The only option that can be true is B: the single proposition from which the process starts contains two terms, its subject and its predicate.

**Answer: B.**

**25.** Identify the pair which is made up of Forms of Opposition:

a) Obversion and Contraposition.
b) Subalternation and Contradiction.
c) Conversion and Contrariety.
d) Subcontrariety and Inversion.

The forms of opposition are contradiction, contrariety, subcontrariety and subalternation. Obversion, contraposition, conversion and inversion are forms of eduction, not of opposition. Only B has two real forms of opposition.

**Answer: B.**

**26.** The relationship between a Universal Affirmative Proposition and a Universal Negative Proposition in Opposition is called:

a) Contrariety.
b) Subalternation.
c) Subcontrariety.
d) Contradictory.

A (All S are P) and E (No S is P) are contraries: they cannot both be true, but they can both be false. Contradictories are A-O and E-I, subcontraries are I-O, and subalterns are A-I and E-O.

**Answer: A.**

**27.** Which of the following Standard Form Categorical Propositions is not convertible in Eduction?

a) Universal Negative
b) Universal Affirmative
c) Particular Negative.
d) Particular Affirmative

Conversion exchanges subject and predicate. E and I convert simply, and A converts by limitation into I (All S are P gives Some P are S). The O proposition cannot be converted at all, because after exchange the new subject would be distributed in the conclusion but was not in the premise (illicit process). So the particular negative is the one that is not convertible.

**Answer: C.**

**28.** The most appropriate usefulness of the Syllogism is that it:

C (precise arguments) and D (clarity in reasoning) both say the same thing in different words, so the question has two defensible answers and cannot be marked reliably.

**Intended answer: it promotes precise argument and clarity in reasoning (C or D).**

The minor term is the subject of the conclusion and it also appears in the minor premise, so it helps to identify the minor premise (the premise that contains it) and also the conclusion. **30.** Which Fallacy is committed in a Syllogistic Argument when a Conclusion is drawn from two Negative Premises?

a) Illicit Major.
b) Illicit Minor.
c) Undistributed Middle.
d) Exclusive Premises.

One rule of the valid syllogism says that no conclusion follows from two negative premises. Breaking it is the fallacy of exclusive premises. Illicit major and illicit minor concern a term distributed in the conclusion but not in its premise, and undistributed middle concerns the middle term.

c) Third Figure.
d) Fourth Figure.

Major term P = eatable things, minor term S = oranges, middle term M = fruits. The major premise is "All M are P" (M-P) and the minor premise is "All S are M" (S-M). The middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise: this is the First Figure (mood AAA, Barbara).

**Answer: A.**

**32.** What is the most adequate Mood of this syllogism below? "No M are P. Some S are M. Therefore, some S are not P"

a) E O O
b) E I I
c) E I O
d) E O I

The mood is the sequence of the types of the major premise, the minor premise and the conclusion. "No M are P" is E, "Some S are M" is I, and "Some S are not P" is O. The mood is EIO (first figure, Ferio), a valid form. A check over all set models confirms that the conclusion cannot fail when both premises hold.

**Answer: C.**

**33.** All of the following Except ONE are requirements for putting Syllogisms into Valid Standard Form:

*Options as printed:* A) Determine the Premise Indicator.   B) Express the Syllogism into Standard Form.   C) Determine the Conclusion Indicator.   D) Respect the Structure of Syllogism.

To put an argument in standard form we find the conclusion (using conclusion indicators such as "therefore"), find the premises (using premise indicators such as "because"), name the major, minor and middle terms, and arrange the major premise, minor premise and conclusion in order while respecting the structure of the syllogism. The printed options mix the steps with the goal itself ("express into standard form" is the aim, not a step), so which one is the "exception" is not determined.

**Intended answer: not determined by the printed options; the steps are identifying the conclusion and premises and respecting the structure of the syllogism.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**34.** In diagramming Categorical Syllogisms, the First circle represents:

*Options as printed:* A) Predicate Term.   B) Middle Term.   C) Major Term.   D) Minor Term.

In a three-circle Venn diagram of a syllogism the circles stand for the minor, major and middle terms, but books differ on which circle is drawn first (the minor term in some, the major term in others), and "Predicate Term" is not a standard name for one of them. The key cannot be settled from the printed paper.

**Intended answer: not determined; the circles represent the minor, major and middle terms, in an order that depends on the textbook.**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**35.** Which part of the Syllogism is omitted in the First order Enthymeme?

a) Minor Premise.
b) Major Premise.
c) Conclusion.
d) Both Premises.

An enthymeme is a syllogism with one part left unstated. By the usual classification, the first-order enthymeme omits the major premise, the second-order omits the minor premise and the third-order omits the conclusion.

**Answer: B.**

**36.** The Syllogism which furnishes the Conclusion for the next Syllogism is known as:

a) Prosyllgism.
b) Episyllogism.
c) Ethymeme.
d) Pollysyllogism.

In a chain of syllogisms (a polysyllogism), the syllogism whose conclusion becomes a premise of the next one is the prosyllogism, and the syllogism that receives that conclusion as a premise is the episyllogism. The printed "Prosyllgism" is a misspelling of prosyllogism.

**Answer: A.**

**37.** Which of the following applies to a Valid Mixed Hypothetical Syllogism (Modus Ponens)?

a) Minor Premise denies antecedent.
b) Conclusion affirms Antecedent.
c) Conclusion affirms Consequent.
d) Minor premise affirms Consequent.

In modus ponens the major premise is "If p then q", the minor premise affirms the antecedent ($p$) and the conclusion affirms the consequent ($q$). Denying the antecedent (A) and affirming the consequent (D) are the two classic fallacies, and B is wrong because the antecedent is affirmed in the minor premise, not in the conclusion.

**Answer: C.**

**38.** Identify the pair below which constitute the types of Disjunctive Syllogism:

a) Modus Tollendo Ponens and Modus Tollendo Ponens.
b) Modus Tollens and Modus Tollendo Ponens.
c) Modus Ponendo Tollens and Modus Ponens.
d) Modus Ponendo Tollens and Modus Tollendo Ponens.

The two types of disjunctive syllogism are modus ponendo tollens (affirming one alternative denies the other, for an exclusive disjunction) and modus tollendo ponens (denying one alternative affirms the other). Modus ponens and modus tollens belong to the hypothetical (conditional) syllogism, and option A repeats the same name twice.

**Answer: D.**

**39.** Determine the Form of the following Dilemma: "If the baby is sick, then he will be admitted in hospital and treated. The baby is neither admitted in hospital nor treated. Therefore, he is not sick"

a) Complex constructive.
b) Simple Destructive.
c) Complex Destructive.
d) Simple Constructive.

The argument has one antecedent ("the baby is sick") and its consequences (admitted, treated) are denied, concluding that the antecedent is false. Denying the consequents to deny the antecedent is the destructive form, and a single antecedent makes it simple: a simple destructive form (modus tollens). A complex form would have two different antecedents and two different consequents.

**Answer: B.**

**40.** Select the importance of the study of Fallacies:

a) Detecting errors in reasoning.
b) Convincing people in Arguments.
c) Knowing good from bad judgment.
d) Misleading people with reasoning.

Studying fallacies trains us to recognise and avoid errors in reasoning. B and D describe misusing arguments, and C is about judgment in general rather than reasoning errors.

**Answer: A.**

**41.** Which of the following pair is made up of Informal Fallacies?

a) Ad Verecundiam and Obscure definition.
b) Undistributed Middle and Accident.
c) Petitio Principii and Accent.
d) Amphiboly and Illicit Process.

Informal fallacies come from the content or language of the argument. Petitio principii (begging the question) and accent (shifting the stress to change the meaning) are both informal fallacies. Undistributed middle and illicit process are formal (structural) fallacies of the syllogism, and obscure definition is a fault of definition, not an informal fallacy of argument.

**Answer: C.**

**42.** "Don't punish this child because he is an IDP", this reasoning commits the Fallacy of:

a) Ad Hominem.
b) Ad Baculum.
c) Ad Populum.
d) Ad Misericordiam.

The speaker asks for pity for the child's situation (an internally displaced person) instead of giving a reason about what he did. Appeal to pity is the fallacy ad misericordiam. Ad hominem attacks the person, ad baculum threatens force and ad populum appeals to the crowd.

**Answer: D.**

**43.** Identify that which best distinguishes the Fallacy of Converse Accident from the Fallacy of Accident:

a) In the latter one moves quickly from generalization to particular case while in the former one moves quickly from particular case to generalization.
b) In the former one moves too quickly from the particular to general case while in the latter one moves too quickly from general case to particular case.
c) In the former one hastily draws a conclusion while in the latter one investigates.
d) In the latter a conclusion is drawn from facts while in the former the conclusion is not drawn from facts.

Accident applies a general rule to a particular case it was not meant for (general to particular). Converse accident (hasty generalisation) draws a general rule from a few particular cases (particular to general). Here "the former" is converse accident and "the latter" is accident, so A is the correct contrast. Option B has them the wrong way round, because it describes accident as the former. C and D do not describe either fallacy.

**Answer: A.**

**44.** The Fallacy of Composition is committed when:

a) One attributes the proprieties of the part to the whole.
b) The Conclusion is irrelevant to the premises.
c) One attributes the properties of the whole to the part.
d) The Conclusion doesn't follow from the premises.

Composition is the move from the parts to the whole: because each part has a property, we wrongly say the whole has it ("each brick is light, so the wall is light"). The reverse, from whole to parts, is the fallacy of division (C).

**Answer: A.**

**45.** The study of Symbolic Logic is of great important because it:

a) Brings obscurity in language.
b) Involves the use of special words.
c) Employs special reasoning.
d) Avoids the vagueness of language.

Symbolic logic replaces ordinary words by precise symbols, so it removes the ambiguity and vagueness of everyday language and makes the structure of an argument clear. It does not add obscurity (A), and special words and special reasoning are not the reason for its value.

**Answer: D.**

**46.** Who amongst these logicians considered Logic and Mathematics as one?

a) George Boole and Whitehead.
b) Aristotle and Whitehead.
c) Bertrand Russell and George Boole.
d) John Venn and Leibniz.

George Boole treated logic as an algebra, and Bertrand Russell (with Whitehead) argued that mathematics can be derived from logic. Together they stand for the view that logic and mathematics are one. Aristotle did not treat logic as mathematics, and Venn is known for his diagrams. Option A gives Whitehead without Russell, who is the leading figure of this thesis.

**Answer: C.**

**47.** Identify the Proposition correctly punctuated below:

*Options as printed:* A) $(p \vee q) \cdot (r \cdot s)$   B) $(p \vee q \cdot r)$   C) $(p \vee q)(r \cdot s)$   D) $(p \vee q) \cdot r)$

A proposition is correctly punctuated when every connective joins well-formed parts and the brackets balance. Option A, $(p \vee q) \cdot (r \cdot s)$, is well formed. Option B is ambiguous (no bracket tells whether the dot or the vee is the main connective), and C has no connective between its two groups. D, as printed, has an unbalanced bracket, but without that stray bracket it would be $(p \vee q) \cdot r$, which is also well formed. Because D can be read as a misprint of a correct form, two answers are defensible.

**Intended answer: A, $(p \vee q) \cdot (r \cdot s)$ (D only if its final bracket is a misprint).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically, so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

**48.** Which of the following rules is applicable to Disjunction?

a) F T = F
b) F F = F
c) T T = F
d) T F = F

A disjunction $p \vee q$ is false only when both disjuncts are false: for $F, F$ the value is $F$. With $F,T$, $T,F$ or $T,T$ it is true (inclusive disjunction).

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \vee q$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | T |
| F | T | T |
| F | F | F |

**Answer: B.**

**49.** Which of the following symbolizes an Implication?

a) $p \cdot q$
b) $p \vee q$
c) $p \supset q$
d) $p \equiv q$

The horseshoe $\supset$ stands for the conditional (implication) "if $p$ then $q$". The dot is conjunction, the vee is disjunction and the triple bar is equivalence.

**Answer: C.**

**50.** How many columns are required in constructing a Truth Table for the Function $(p \equiv q)$?

a) Four
b) Two
c) Six
d) Three

The table needs one column for each distinct variable and one for the function itself: a column for $p$, a column for $q$ and a column for $p \equiv q$, which makes three columns (and four rows).

| $p$ | $q$ | $p \equiv q$ |
|---|---|---|
| T | T | T |
| T | F | F |
| F | T | F |
| F | F | T |

**Answer: D.**

« Igname » est ici employé au pluriel, sans détermination précise : il faut l’article indéfini pluriel « des ». « De l’ » est un partitif singulier devant voyelle, « les » est défini, « l’ » est singulier. Règle : quantité indéterminée de choses comptables au pluriel = « des ». **Réponse : B.**

b) à le

**3.** Mon camarade a été exclu de notre établissement car il devait reprendre la classe de Form4 à 21 ans. 21 en lettres s’écrit comme suit :
